title: Start here
objective: Call whether an agent's transfer can overdraw the sender, then read what the solver finds and what its answer is about.

blocks.md:
An agent opened a pull request on your system. Its description says: "Transfer is now guarded; safe, 200 tests green." That is the agent's text, quoted and unreviewed. Here is the change.

```python
def transfer(src, dst, amount):
    if amount <= 0 or amount > dst.balance:   # "guard: sufficient funds"
        raise Rejected
    src.balance -= amount
    dst.balance += amount
```

You will make a call before anything answers: your verdict, and how sure you are, committed first. Then Z3, a solver, checks every whole-number input at once.
The same transfer, written as a search for a bug.
blocks.direction: Query asserts: balances and an amount that pass the guard as written and leave the sender below zero. `sat` means Z3 found such a transfer, and the model shows it.

code.text:
from z3 import *
a, b, amount = Ints('a b amount')   # sender, recipient, amount
s = Solver()
s.add(a >= 0, b >= 0, amount > 0)   # balances start at zero or above
s.add(amount <= b)                  # the guard, as the pull request wrote it
s.add(a - amount < 0)               # the bug to find: the sender ends below zero
print(s.check())
print(s.model())

tap.property: the sender never ends below zero

call.prompt: Can the sender's balance go below zero after this transfer, for some whole-number balances?

options.text: No: the guard checks funds before the debit.
options.why: The guard reads `dst`, so it checks the wrong balance. Green tests sample inputs, and tests that give both accounts the same balance never reach this case.

options.text: Yes: a counterexample gets past the guard.
options.why: Z3 searched every whole-number input and found one that passes the guard and overdraws the sender.

options.text: Only when the amount exceeds both balances.
options.why: An amount above both balances fails the guard. The bad inputs are those where the recipient covers the amount and the sender does not.

blocks.after:
Z3 found a transfer that passes the guard and overdraws the sender: the sender holds 0, the recipient holds 1, and the amount is 1 {{run:RUN-z3-boot-variant}}. Your model may differ, because any transfer that passes the guard and overdraws the sender will do.

The guard reads `dst`, the recipient, so it checks the wrong balance. Tests that give both accounts the same balance cannot tell the two guards apart, which is how a suite like this one stays green {{run:RUN-z3-boot-variant}}.

blocks.md: That model is a specimen: a counterexample you keep beside its fix. The fix is one word. The guard should read the sender, `src`, not the recipient, `dst`.
The same search, with the guard fixed.
blocks.direction: Query asserts: the same search, with the guard reading the sender. `unsat` means Z3 found no such transfer.

code.text:
from z3 import *
a, b, amount = Ints('a b amount')
s = Solver()
s.add(a >= 0, b >= 0, amount > 0)
s.add(amount <= a)                  # the fix: the guard reads the sender
s.add(a - amount < 0)
print(s.check())

tap.property: the sender never ends below zero

blocks.after:
Z3 found no transfer that passes this guard and overdraws the sender {{run:RUN-z3-boot-variant}}.

Now read the stamp under the cell. A stamp is a word plus a code that says what a check established, with its qualifier. This one reads PROVED [P] · Z3 5.3.1 unsat · uncertified. Its plain line says: for whole numbers; sender only; the encoding is not yet checked against your code.

That is the whole loop: call it, read the witness, fix the guard, read the stamp.

blocks.md: The stamp said "for whole numbers". Most code keeps balances in 64 bits, and 64-bit arithmetic wraps around. Here is the fixed guard again with 64-bit balances. There is no call this time, so just look.
The fixed guard, on 64-bit numbers, with a search for a recipient who ends below zero.
blocks.direction: Query asserts: the fixed guard on 64-bit numbers, and a recipient who ends below zero after the credit. `sat` means Z3 found one.

code.text:
from z3 import *
A, B, X = BitVecs('A B X', 64)        # 64-bit balances and amount
s = Solver()
s.add(A >= 0, B >= 0, X > 0, X <= A)  # the fixed guard
s.add(B + X < 0)                      # the recipient ends below zero
print(s.check())
print(s.model())

tap.property: the recipient never ends below zero

blocks.after: Z3 found one {{run:RUN-z3-bv64}}. In the recorded result the recipient holds 9223372036850581504 and the amount is 4194304, and together they read as a negative number. Your model may differ, because any pair that wraps will do. The same guard still protects the sender when the amount is positive {{run:RUN-z3-bv64}}.

blocks.md: The guard protects the sender, not the recipient.

blocks.title: Bitcoin, August 2010
blocks.md: On 2010-08-15 it was found that Bitcoin's transaction checks "didn't account for the case of outputs so large that they overflowed when summed". A transaction in block 74638 had created 184,467,440,737.09551616 bitcoins. Source: the Bitcoin wiki page for CVE-2010-5139, read 2026-10-23.

blocks.title: This will feel harder
blocks.md: Effortful practice often feels slower than rereading, and it tends to stick better. Expect that here.

Pick a range of hours you can give this, such as 6 to 10 a week. Put two study blocks at your laptop in it, and one Keep block. A Keep block holds your Today sessions. Today is a practice session of 10 to 12 minutes, three to five times a week, and it starts with a fresh transfer to call, on the move the next lesson teaches.

Already know some logic? An optional placement walk lets the course skip what you show. You can take it whenever you like.

notes: Recorded by W1-T12. values.queries.<query> holds each query's verdict and rlimit; for a sat query, its witness (the primary configuration's model, as strings), the text of the primary configuration's replay (replay) and whether every configuration's model for it replayed (witness_replays); its unsat_core or minimum where it has one; the SHA-256 of its SMT-LIB export; and the verdict of each configuration that ran it (engines, cvc5's on the 5 queries it ran). Cite one as {{run:RUN-z3-boot-variant#values.queries.<name>.verdict}}. 5 queries in all.

Where each configuration ran: native, pyodide-node, pyodide-chromium, pyodide-firefox, pyodide-webkit, cvc5-bench. native is the host under uv (CPython 3.13, the wheel z3_solver-5.3.1.0-py3-none-manylinux_2_27_x86_64.whl from PyPI, no container); pyodide-node is Pyodide 314.0.7 with the z3_solver 5.3.1.0 pyemscripten wheel under Node 22 on the host (CPython 3.14 inside Pyodide); the pyodide-chromium, pyodide-firefox and pyodide-webkit configurations are the same engine in a module worker of each browser inside the pinned Playwright container (desktop builds, headless, not phones); cvc5-bench is cvc5 1.4.2, the Bench binary, in the Bench image with the network off.

Witnesses are recorded by property and never compared by value across engines [X RUN-z3-bv64-pyodide]: every sat query's model is replayed in plain Python integers by the script itself, in each configuration that gave one (native, pyodide-node, pyodide-chromium, pyodide-firefox and pyodide-webkit; cvc5-bench gives verdicts only), and the check is that every one of them replays. In this run the configurations in values.engines returned the same model for every sat query, which is a fact about this run and no promise.

Every query ran with rlimit 5000000 (spine section 9.1; values.queries.<query>.rlimit). The SMT-LIB exports are Z3's to_smt2() text with its let names (?x60, $x34) renamed in order of appearance, because Z3 names them after AST ids and the ids are not the same in every process: in this record the raw text of every export happened to be identical in every Z3 configuration. The renamed text is the same in every Z3 configuration, and its SHA-256 is values.queries.<query>.smt2_sha256.

started_at and duration_s of a configuration that ran its own command (native, pyodide-node and cvc5-bench) are when that command started and how long it took, start-up included. Each browser configuration (pyodide-chromium, pyodide-firefox and pyodide-webkit) comes from one docker run, in which one browser session ran every Z3 script of runs/inputs/S1 in turn; that session is shared by the 9 Z3 records of runs/inputs/S1, and the configuration's argv and exit_code are its docker run's. A browser configuration's started_at is when its session began, after the browser had launched and before its page opened, and its duration_s is this script's own time in the worker, measured around the call without the engine's start-up and rounded to whole milliseconds by the harness. Its environment holds two spans that cover every script: session_wall_ms, from started_at to when the last script had finished (the page's and the engine's load and every script, not the browser's close), and docker_run_wall_ms, the docker run from docker_run_started_at, when the recording script started it, to its exit (adding the container's start and the launch of Node and the browser before started_at, and the browser's close and the output's chown after the last script). budget.harness_timeout_s is the wall time after which the recording script would have stopped a configuration's command (for a browser configuration, the docker run). The ms figure on an @@ line is the script's own measurement of that query's solver call, rounded to hundredths of a millisecond; in this record's browser logs pyodide-firefox and pyodide-webkit gave whole milliseconds, and pyodide-chromium gave multiples of 0.1 ms, on all 5 queries, so a browser figure of a few milliseconds is a rough one.

cvc5 1.4.2 [git 282d5e0 on branch HEAD] ran 5 of the 5 queries, each file under a 60 s limit (budget.per_file_timeout_s): every sat or unsat query that has an SMT-LIB export, as that text, which here is every query. The checks require its verdict to equal Z3's on each one it ran (values.cvc5, and engines in each entry).

In native and pyodide-node, which ran on the host, argv's paths to the script are relative to a scratch folder that held copies of the configuration's inputs from runs/inputs/S1/RUN-z3-boot-variant/ at the same relative paths, and the command ran in that folder; pyodide-node.mjs is named by its path from the repository root, and the <sandbox> paths are placeholders (next note).

Placeholders in argv: <sandbox>/engines is a scratch directory with Pyodide's npm package unpacked in pyodide/ and the Z3 wheel, both fetched and checked against their published digests (the inputs list them); <sandbox>/out is the browser container's output directory; <sandbox>/smt2 is a scratch copy of the SMT-LIB files the cvc5 configuration reads (the inputs list them). Repository paths are relative to the repository root.
